card.name: Nati
card.tagline: A winding mountain circle dance linked across the valleys of Himachal Pradesh.
card.profile: Nati is a community folk dance native to Himachal Pradesh and the Western and Central Hills of the Indian subcontinent, performed across Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Chamba, and Kinnaur. Moving in circles or semi-circles to the percussive pulse of dhol-damau, shehnai, and curved horns, dancers link hands with alternate partners in a distinct criss-cross grip or sway their hands freely tracing figure eights. While historically performed by men, women now prominently lead and maintain the tradition during births, weddings, harvests, and religious festivals. The dance follows an eight-step framework that begins at a slow pace and gradually accelerates alongside the music, closing with a sacred yagna whenever staged for temple deities.
card.insight: On 26 October 2015, exactly 9,892 women in vibrant Kullvi dress danced Nati together at the International Dussehra festival, entering the Guinness Book of World Records as the world's largest folk dance.
card.profile_long:
Nati is the traditional folk dance of the Western and Central Hills of the Indian subcontinent, deeply rooted in the rugged valleys of Himachal Pradesh. Documented across districts including Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Chamba, and Kinnaur, Nati has also spread into the plainlands through pahari migration. Historically danced by men, women have taken a primary role in carrying the tradition forward in contemporary community life. The choreography draws inspiration from regional devotional lore, specifically the stories of Raaslila and Chandravali, uniting villagers across generations in shared kinetic rhythm.

The performance unfolds without strict limits on participant numbers, gathering dancers into expansive circles or curving semi-circles that drift gently forward and backward. Formation lines are arranged either with men and women alternating or with full single-gender segments side by side. Dancers frequently grasp the hands of alternate partners to forge a visual criss-cross weave, though they may also dance with unknitted hands, swaying their arms through the air while curling their palms into the shape of a horizontal figure eight. Leadership falls to male dancers positioned at the head of the line carrying a chowrie (fly whisk) or dangru (axe). The core technique rests upon a foundational sequence of eight coordinated footsteps shared across valleys, beginning in a gentle, languid cadence and gathering speed as the percussion accelerates.

Music forms an inseparable architecture for the steps, driven by traditional instrumentalists known locally as tunis. The primary rhythm is struck on percussion instruments including dhol, damau, and nagara, while wind melodies are sounded by the shehnai and resounding brass horns like the longish karnal and the curved narsingha or narsinghe. Lyrical lines sung during the dance weave old folklore into contemporary celebrations. The musical arrangement paces the ritual gathering, beginning with measured restraint before urging the circle into faster momentum.

Costume and adornment provide regional identity across the Himachal hills. Men traditionally wear Himachali woollen caps (topis), fitted woollen pants (suthan), a kurta, and a Nehru jacket wrapped at the waist with a muffler or gachi. In Kinnaur, topis are decorated with local flowers and seeds of the Indian trumpet tree; in Kullu, headwear features woven flower garlands; and in Sirmaur, men wear swirling tunics called choltu. Women dress in suit-salwar with a sadri jacket, a dhattu headscarf, and a gachi waist sash, accessorised with ornaments such as chandrahaar, bumni, and jhanjhar. Kullu women drape a distinct one-piece woollen wrap known as pattu, whereas dancers in Shimla favour the rezta, a long traditional skirt-and-blouse ensemble now popular throughout the state. Both men and women wear handmade grass-and-cloth footwear known as pullas and frequently tie a handkerchief to their right index finger.

Nati marks life-cycle ceremonies, including births and weddings, alongside seasonal agrarian celebrations like crop harvests and sacred festivals such as Dussehra and Diwali. While embraced as a celebratory community gathering, it maintains deep ties to Hindu deities; whenever staged on sacred occasions, performers conclude the gathering with a yagna sacrifice to pay homage to the gods. Sirmouri Nati troupes directed by figures such as Dr. Joginder Singh Habbi have achieved national and international records, while in Kullu on 26 October 2015, a massive gathering of 9,892 women performed simultaneously, earning Nati recognition in the Guinness Book of World Records as the largest folk dance in the world.

sections.origins_and_history: Nati originated in the Western and Central Hills of the Indian subcontinent as a community tradition native to Himachal Pradesh, with historical roots across Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Chamba, and Kinnaur. Historically danced exclusively by male villagers, women have increasingly become the primary practitioners sustaining the form. Due to regional migration of pahari communities, the dance has also established popularity across the plainlands.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers arrange themselves in open circles or semi-circles without participant limits, moving forward and backward in coordinated lines. Performers either hold hands with alternate partners to form a criss-cross pattern or sway their hands freely through the air, turning their palms into a horizontal figure-eight motion. Group lines are led by male dancers brandishing a fly whisk (chowrie) or an axe (dangru). While regional variations exist, all styles share a core baseline of eight coordinated footsteps that start slowly and accelerate as the music quickens.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performances are accompanied by traditional musicians known as tunis, playing regional percussion and wind instruments. The rhythmic core is maintained by dhol, damau, and nagara drums, complemented by the melodic tones of the shehnai and brass wind instruments including the longish karnal horn and curved narsingha (narsinghe). The songs carry traditional narrative folklore and dictate the tempo shifts of the line.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes vary by district across Himachal Pradesh. Male attire includes Himachali topis (caps), fitted woollen suthan trousers, kurtas, Nehru jackets, and gachi waist sashes, with Kinnaur dancers adorning topis with flowers and Indian trumpet seeds, Sirmaur men wearing choltu tunics, and Kullu men wearing flower garland headwear. Women wear suit-salwar or rezta dresses, sadri vests, dhattu headscarves, and regional jewellery including chandrahaar, bumni, and jhanjhar, with Kullu women donning pattu drapes. Dancers wear handmade pulla footwear and often knot a handkerchief around their right index finger.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Nati is performed across community and religious celebrations, including births, weddings, harvest gatherings, and major festivals such as Diwali and Dussehra. The dance draws thematic meaning from Vaishnava devotional narratives of Raaslila and Chandravali. When held as part of sacred religious events, dancers conclude the performance with a formal yagna fire ritual to honour local Hindu deities.
sections.notable_figures: Dr. Joginder Singh Habbi directed the Sirmour District cultural group, achieving ten consecutive folk dance competition victories and entering Sirmouri Natti into the India Book of Records, Asia Book of Records, and the World Book of Records.
sections.regional_variants: Distinct regional forms include Kullvi Nati, Mahasuvi Nati, Sirmauri Nati, Kinnauri Nati (noted for mime-like, languid sequences), Jaunpuri Nati, Barada Nati, and Bangani Nati. It is also known as Tandi in Jaunsar-Bawar. People of the Lahaul district practise their own dance, Garphi, and Nati is not part of Lahauli culture.
sections.lineage: Nati's expressive choreography is rooted in narratives of the Hindu deity traditions of Raaslila and Chandravali, carried forward across generations in the Himalayan valleys through family, festive, and village temple gatherings.

claims.text: Nati is a folk dance native to Himachal Pradesh in the Western and Central Hills of the Indian subcontinent.
Nati is danced in districts such as Kullu, Mandi, Shimla, Sirmaur, Chamba, and Kinnaur.
The dance is performed to percussion beats supplied by instruments known as dhol-damau.
Kinnauri Nati includes languid sequences and has a mime-like quality.
The people of Lahaul district practise their own distinct dance called Garphi, and Nati is not part of their culture.
The choreography draws inspiration from devotional lore involving Raaslila and Chandravali.
On sacred occasions, a yagna is conducted at the close of the dance to pay homage to deities.
The dance relies on a universal baseline of 8 steps executed at a slow tempo.
On 26 October 2015, a world record was set when 9,892 women performed Nati together during the International Dussehra festival.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Valley of Ten Thousand Dancers
episode_brief.logline: Across the high cedar hills of Himachal Pradesh, thousands of dancers knit hands in a slow, winding circle that builds to an ecstatic village celebration.
beats: Opening on the high ridge of Kullu during Dussehra as tuni musicians raise long karnal horns to the sky.
A leader steps forward carrying a silver dangru axe, guiding the initial slow footsteps of the circle.
Dancers weave their fingers into the alternate criss-cross grip, showing the contrast of vibrant pattu drapes and embroidered topis.
The camera steps inside the Shimla courtyards where women demonstrate the delicate figure-eight palm sway.
Tempo accelerates as the dhol-damau percussion quickens, carrying hundreds of linked dancers through the foundational eight counts.
The dance concludes before a temple hearth as performers assemble for a yagna offering.
visual_motifs: Interlocked hands creating a criss-cross pattern along the circle
Embroidered Himachali topis adorned with wild trumpet tree seeds and marigolds
Handkerchief fluttering from the right index finger during circular turns
Long brass karnal horns pointed upward against Himalayan slopes
